title: Effective one-body interactions due to the presence of a liquid-vapor interface
abstract: In this study we investigate the behavior of additive binary square-well mixtures within the framework of classical density functional theory. By leveraging on the geometrical structure of the square-well interaction, we propose a novel form of the perturbation theory contribution to the density functional in terms of weighted densities, inspired by fundamental measure theory. We apply this functional in order to study the effective one-body interaction due to the liquid-vapor interface of the solvent acting on a dilute component of dissolved nano particles. The effective one-body interaction attracts the nano particles strongly to the interface. We show that this effective interaction potential can be calculated either from the density profiles of the full mixture, at low but non-vanishing concentrations of the nano particles, or by employing the Widom insertion theorem in the dilute limit of vanishing density of nano particles. Both routes display excellent agreement.
summary: This paper uses Density Functional Theory to model a binary mixture near a liquid-vapor interface. It calculates the effective interaction potential acting on dissolved nanoparticles, demonstrating strong attraction to the interface using two consistent theoretical approaches. The work advances understanding of interfacial thermodynamics in soft matter systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the effective one-body interaction experienced by a dilute component (nano particles) due to the presence of a liquid-vapor interface formed by the solvent.
main_result: The calculated effective interaction strongly attracts nano particles to the liquid-vapor interface, and this result is confirmed using two independent theoretical routes.
method: Classical Density Functional Theory (cDFT) is employed, utilizing novel perturbation theory contributions inspired by Fundamental Measure Theory (FMT).
model_or_system: The system modeled is an additive binary square-well mixture containing a solvent undergoing phase separation and dissolved nano particles. The analysis focuses on the density profiles near the planar free interface.

main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the square-well potential model and assumes the neglect of two- and higher order terms in certain theoretical mappings.

paper_structure: The paper introduces DFT for the model system, discusses bulk considerations and phase equilibrium, and then details the calculation of the effective interaction using both direct profile analysis and the Widom insertion theorem.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluids, the rigorous application of advanced statistical mechanics tools like FMT and the Widom theorem to inhomogeneous systems provides methodological insights applicable to quantum many-body problems involving interfaces or confinement.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Liquid-vapor phase separation of the SW binary mixture with corresponding interface (green vertical line) located at z = 0 and density profiles of the first component (black solid) and the second component (dashed blue) which we magnified for visualization. The SW parameters of the second component are chosen to be βε2 = 0.6 and λ2 = 1.5 with σ2/σ1 = 1.

Figure 2: Normalized density profile ρ2(z)/ρ2,0 of the second component at the interface z = 0 for three energies ε2 with range λ2 = 1.5 and size ratio σ2/σ1 = 1. For reasons of clarity we do not show the density profile of the solvent. The lowest value of ε2 corresponds to the case of (slightly) solvophobic nano particles, that prefer the vapor phase, while the highest value of ε2 corresponds to case of (slightly) solvophilic nano particles, which prefer the liquid phase. In the case in between neither the liquid nor the vapor phase is prefered by the nano particles.

Figure 3: Normalized density profiles ρ2(z)/ρ2,0 for several size ratios σ2/σ1 = 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and energies ε2 slightly below (dotted blue) and above (dashed red) the sym- metric solutions (solid black). By increasing the size ratio the adsorption at the interface be- comes stronger and enhances the density by several orders of magnitude. Note the logarithmic scaling of the ordinates.

Figure 4: Effective potential Veff(z) near the interface at z = 0 once obtained via Eq.(35) (red dots) and Eq.(36) (solid black) of the asymmetric mixture σ2/σ1 = 2 evaluated for the symmet- ric case βε2 = 1.3918 (a) and the case βε2 = 1.50 (b) where the nano particles prefer the liquid. The agreement between both routes is very good.
